title: theDECISIONS
note: Every decision about theOS, numbered. A later decision names the one it supersedes.

decisions.title: theBRAIN is native HTML, CSS, JS and JSON
decisions.decision: Docs, wiki and architecture in theOS/theBRAIN are written as HTML, CSS, JS and JSON. No markdown.
decisions.why: One format that the app renders directly, nothing to convert, nothing to drift.

decisions.title: Signers act, identities own
decisions.decision: A signer is a device key (a passkey). It only signs, for an identity, and never owns anything. Only identities own data.
decisions.why: Devices come and go; ownership must not move with them.

decisions.title: Two kinds of identity: human and coop
decisions.decision: A human identity is controlled by signers only. A coop identity is controlled by one or more identities (human or coop), never by signers directly. Cycles are not allowed.
decisions.why: Families, teams and organisations are identities of identities; one model covers all of them.

decisions.title: Data owns itself: the seal
decisions.decision: Data is born with a fresh key pair, the seal. Its public key is the data ID. It signs exactly one thing, the first rule, and the private key is wiped.
decisions.why: Nobody holds the seal, so it cannot be shared, lost or stolen. Keyhive does the same with its genesis key.

decisions.title: One owner per piece of data, and it is an identity
decisions.decision: The seal's first rule names exactly one owner: an identity, human or coop. The owner may do everything, its rule never expires, and only the owner can hand ownership to another identity. The owner is not a role.
decisions.why: A role of owners cannot shrink durably: any past owner could revoke the others for good (Keyline's warning). With one owner identity, people change inside the coop, not in the data.

decisions.title: Rules go to roles, never to identities
decisions.decision: Everyone except the owner gets access through roles. A role is a set of identities. Rules attach only to roles.
decisions.why: People come and go; roles stay. Changing who is in a role never touches the data's rules.

decisions.title: People see "rules"; underneath they are capabilities
decisions.decision: The word everyone sees is "rule". Underneath, each rule is a signed capability token that carries its own proof back to the seal and is checked offline.
decisions.why: "Rule" is the word ordinary people understand; capabilities are what makes it hold without a server.

decisions.title: A rule lists what a role may do
decisions.decision: A rule is: role, data, a "do" list, conditions, expiry. The do list: create, read, update, delete, admin, share, want, keep, sync.
decisions.why: One small vocabulary for content, carrying and the rules themselves. Keyhive's Relay, Read, Edit and Admin map onto it; ours is finer.

decisions.title: Sharing only narrows
decisions.decision: Whoever may share hands on a rule that is the same or smaller: fewer dos, shorter expiry, more conditions. Never more.
decisions.why: Attenuation keeps delegation safe without asking anyone. Meadowcap and Biscuit both require each step to sit inside the previous one.

decisions.title: Read is encryption, everything else is verification
decisions.decision: Reading is enforced by keys. Every other do is enforced by every peer checking each signed change against the rules in the history.
decisions.why: Encryption can only be all or nothing per key; signature checks can be as fine as needed.

decisions.title: Reading is per piece of data; changes can be as fine as needed
decisions.decision: Read is granted per piece of data. Anything to be shared on its own is its own data. Create, update and delete can be narrowed to paths and matching entries.
decisions.why: A reader holds the plaintext, so finer read limits would be promises, not protection.

decisions.title: Every rule expires and renews itself
decisions.decision: Rules expire after 30 days unless set otherwise. An admin's device renews unchanged rules a week before they end. The owner's first rule never expires.
decisions.why: Forgotten shares close by themselves; families are never locked out.

decisions.title: Endings: revoke and lapse
decisions.decision: A revoke (by an admin) and a lapse (by any peer, once the date has passed) are the same kind of event in the history. An ending wins over every change that never saw it, turns the data key, and is the delete trigger on honest devices.
decisions.why: Validity follows from the history alone, so all copies agree. No clock is trusted.
decisions.rejected: Checking expiry against each device's own clock (copies would disagree).

decisions.title: Ambiguity resolves toward less authority
decisions.decision: When rule changes and other changes are concurrent, the result with less authority wins.
decisions.why: The safe default without a central order. Keyhive's guiding rule.

decisions.title: A removed admin means a successor role
decisions.decision: When an admin is removed from a role, the role is replaced by a successor with a new ID and the remaining members are added again.
decisions.why: A removed admin can backdate a revoke by pretending not to have seen their removal. Old revokes then point at a dead role.

decisions.title: Keys: identity key, role key, data key
decisions.decision: Content is encrypted with a data key. The data key is wrapped for the owner and for each reading role. The role key is wrapped for each member's identity key. Each new data key opens the previous one.
decisions.why: Envelope encryption is the proven pattern (HPKE; Keybase teams, Jazz, Cryptree). Removing a member rotates one role key, not every piece of data. Forward secrecy is given up on purpose, because CRDTs need their whole history.

sources.label: Keyhive notebook 06: E2EE in the local-first setting

decisions.title: The keyring travels with the data
decisions.decision: Each piece of data carries its keyring (envelopes, epoch, back-links) next to its rules, sealed.
decisions.why: No one keeps keys for the data; it is self-contained wherever it goes.

decisions.title: Which key turns when
decisions.decision: Adding a member or giving read: nothing turns. Removing a member: new role key, data keys on next write. Removing an admin: successor role. Taking read: new data key now. Stolen device: identity key and every role it is in. Concurrent rotations are both kept until the next one.
decisions.why: Only read touches keys; the rest is signed rules.

decisions.title: Envelopes only for published, signed locks
decisions.decision: Each device derives its encryption key (lock) from its passkey's PRF secret and publishes it in its identity's history, signed by its signer. Envelopes are made only for locks found there, and only by someone a rule allows.
decisions.why: Stops an attacker from slipping in a lock of their own. Closes the gap Keyhive lists as G2.

decisions.title: BeeKEM inside large roles, later
decisions.decision: Small roles use one envelope per member. Roles of several dozen members and up manage their role key with BeeKEM. Not per piece of data.
decisions.why: BeeKEM per document (Keyhive) costs one update per document a removed reader could read; per role it costs one. Every Keyhive crate is pre-alpha and unaudited: pin and audit before use.

decisions.title: Data is a Doc or a Value
decisions.decision: A Doc is JSON that changes, made of CRDT data types (Loro underneath). A Value is bytes that never change, named by their BLAKE3 hash, streamed in checked chunks. Every Value has a small metadata Doc that holds its key.
decisions.why: Mergeable structure where it helps, plain files where it does not.

decisions.title: Words: do, op, change
decisions.decision: A do is what you ask the engine to do. An op is a CRDT op, as in Loro. Rules list dos. The slides name CRDT data types, not Loro.
decisions.why: One meaning per word.

decisions.title: The engine: JSON dos, pluggable, local
decisions.decision: Every read, change, search and sync is a JSON do (find, walk, search, near, chain …). New kinds plug in and name what a rule must allow. Dos run only on your own device, over what you can read.
decisions.why: One engine for everything, with no server in the loop.

decisions.title: Peers sync, they never ask
decisions.decision: No peer ever answers questions about its data for another peer. Peers only carry what rules allow. A shared answer is its own data with its own rule.
decisions.why: Removes the trust in the answering device, and the risk of asking one's way to the content.

decisions.title: Rules are their own signed set, not a Loro doc
decisions.decision: Rules, role memberships and endings are a grow-only set of signed certificates, merged by union and evaluated by our own logic.
decisions.why: Rule conflicts need "less authority wins"; Loro's last-writer-wins would resolve them wrongly. Keyhive does the same.

decisions.title: Sealed in chunks, linked by hashes
decisions.decision: Devices seal ranges of changes (Loro update bytes, compressed, then encrypted). Boundaries come from change hashes so every device cuts the same way; small chunks merge into bigger ones over time. Each chunk is hashed and lists the chunks before it; its signed header binds Loro's peer ID to the signer.
decisions.why: Sealing op by op makes data huge and uncompressible. Same lesson as Keyhive's sedimentree.

decisions.title: Carriers see sealed chunks and proofs, never rules
decisions.decision: Rules are sealed for readers. A carrier checks only proofs: the asker's want proof, and each change author's proof. IDs in proofs are pseudonymous.
decisions.why: Keyhive syncs its membership graph to servers in plain text; we keep that private too.

decisions.title: Peer to peer over iroh
decisions.decision: Devices connect directly over iroh: the address is a key, relays see only sealed traffic. Each device's iroh key is separate from its signer and vouched for by it.
decisions.why: No cloud in the middle; the address can change without touching the identity.

decisions.title: Evaluate Subduction for sync
decisions.decision: Test Ink & Switch's Subduction (iroh transport, sedimentree, RIBLT set reconciliation) before building our own sync.
decisions.why: It already syncs encrypted history between peers that cannot read it, and finds differences at about 1.5 summaries per missing item.
